lessons.title: Lab: Variables, arrays, hashtables

scenes.text: Your manager wants 'a list of servers with their owners'. You keep it in PowerShell, not in your head.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body: `$servers = 'FS01','FS02','APP07'` is an array; `$servers.Count` → 3; `$servers[0]` → FS01. A hashtable maps keys to values: `$owner = @{FS01='Files team'; APP07='ERP team'}`; `$owner['APP07']`.

steps.title: Objects
steps.body: `[pscustomobject]@{Name='FS01'; FreeGB=61.4}` makes a real object you can sort, filter and export. Strings: double quotes expand variables ("Server $s"), single quotes don't.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: `$d = Get-PSDrive C; [math]::Round($d.Free/1GB,1)` gives free GB with one decimal.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: `$a = 'FS01, FS02'` is ONE string, not an array; using single quotes when you meant to expand a variable.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone: stale computer accounts report

scenes.text: Audit says AD has ~600 computer accounts, but only ~420 devices exist. You must report stale ones (no logon for 90 days) — not delete them.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: lastLogonTimestamp
steps.body: Replicated attribute, updated only when older than ~14 days (msDS-LogonTimeSyncInterval default) — accurate enough for 90-day staleness. `Get-ADComputer -Filter * -Properties LastLogonDate` exposes it as a date.

steps.title: Script
steps.body: `$cut = (Get-Date).AddDays(-90); Get-ADComputer -Filter 'Enabled -eq $true' -Properties LastLogonDate,OperatingSystem | Where-Object { $_.LastLogonDate -lt $cut } | Select Name,OperatingSystem,LastLogonDate | Sort LastLogonDate | Export-Csv C:\Reports\stale-computers.csv -NoTypeInformation`

steps.title: Safe cleanup
steps.body: Report → owner review → disable and move to a Stale OU (with date in description) → delete after e.g. 30 more days. Never delete servers/cluster objects from a script without review.

lessons.title: Lab: Schedule a script with Task Scheduler

scenes.text: The low-disk report from the scripting course must run every weekday at 06:00 without anyone logged in.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

lessons.title: Lab: Group Managed Service Accounts

scenes.text: Security forbids personal or shared passwords in scheduled tasks. Use a gMSA.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: gMSA
steps.body: AD generates and rotates a long random password automatically (default every 30 days); only allowed computers can retrieve it. One-time per forest: a **KDS root key** (`Add-KdsRootKey -EffectiveImmediately`, then allow time to replicate — Microsoft documents waiting up to 10 hours before use in production).

steps.title: Steps
steps.body: `New-ADServiceAccount -Name gmsa-reports -DNSHostName gmsa-reports.contoso.local -PrincipalsAllowedToRetrieveManagedPassword 'ADM01$'` → on ADM01: `Install-ADServiceAccount gmsa-reports` → `Test-ADServiceAccount gmsa-reports` (True) → task principal `New-ScheduledTaskPrincipal -UserId 'CONTOSO\gmsa-reports$' -LogonType Password`. Grant the gMSA only the rights it needs (e.g. Modify on \\FS01\Reports).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the trailing $ in the account name; giving the gMSA Domain Admin 'to make it work'.

lessons.title: Lab: Logging: transcripts and verbose output

scenes.text: The task 'failed' last night. Without logs, nobody knows why.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: Patterns
steps.body: Start every unattended script with `Start-Transcript -Path "C:\Logs\lowdisk-$(Get-Date -f yyyyMMdd-HHmm).log"` and end with `Stop-Transcript`. Use `Write-Verbose` for detail (enabled with -Verbose) and `Write-Warning`/`Write-Error` for problems; `exit 1` on failure so LastTaskResult shows it.

steps.title: Retention
steps.body: Delete logs older than N days at the start of the script so logs don't fill the disk.

steps.title: How L2/L3 engineers approach it
steps.body:
- Define scope first: one user, one site, or everyone?
- Ask **what changed** (changes, patches, moves) — most incidents follow a change.
- Gather evidence at each layer before acting and keep a timestamped work log.
- Escalate early with facts when the fix needs rights or a change you don't own.

lessons.title: Disks, partitions and file systems

story.title: A 4 TB disk shows as 2 TB

scenes.text: A new 4 TB disk on FS02 only offers 2 TB in Disk Management. Someone initialised it as MBR.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: Partition styles
steps.body: **MBR**: max 2 TiB per disk addressable (with 512-byte sectors), up to 4 primary partitions. **GPT**: required for UEFI boot, supports huge disks and up to 128 partitions in Windows.

steps.title: File systems
steps.body: **NTFS**: permissions, compression, EFS, quotas, dedup — the default. **ReFS**: resilience (integrity streams), great for Hyper-V VHDX and backup repositories; not bootable for the OS, some NTFS features missing (e.g. EFS, disk quotas).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Converting MBR→GPT on a disk with data using Disk Management (it requires wiping; use MBR2GPT only for OS disks under supported conditions).

statements.s: MBR disks can address at most about 2 TiB with 512-byte sectors.
ReFS is the recommended file system for the Windows OS boot volume.
GPT is required to boot in UEFI mode.

lessons.title: Lab: Bring a new disk online

steps.title: Commands

story.title: 'The file or directory is corrupted and unreadable'

scenes.text: A user gets a corruption error on a share. System log shows Ntfs Event 55.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: Online first
steps.body: `chkdsk D: /scan` runs online (no dismount) and queues issues; `chkdsk D: /spotfix` fixes queued issues with a very short dismount; `/f` and `/r` need exclusive access (a reboot for C:) and `/r` reads every sector — hours on big volumes.

steps.title: Hardware health
steps.body: `Get-PhysicalDisk | Select FriendlyName,HealthStatus,OperationalStatus` and `Get-StorageReliabilityCounter` for physical servers; for VMs, involve the storage/virtualisation team.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Running `chkdsk /r` on a 10 TB file server volume during business hours.

lessons.title: Lab: RPO, RTO and the 3-2-1 rule

scenes.text: The file server is backed up every 4 hours (00, 04, 08…). It dies at 11:55. How much work is lost?
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body: **RPO** (Recovery Point Objective): the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time. **RTO** (Recovery Time Objective): the maximum acceptable time to restore service. Backup frequency must be ≤ RPO; restore procedures and hardware must meet RTO.

steps.title: Worked example
steps.body: Backups at 08:00 and 12:00. Failure at 11:55 → last good point 08:00 → **3 h 55 min** of changes lost (worst case approaches the 4-hour interval).
3 copies of data, on 2 different media/types, 1 off-site; modern variants add 1 offline/immutable copy and 0 errors in restore tests — the defence against ransomware deleting backups.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Never testing restores; backups on the same storage as production; backup admin accounts that are ordinary domain admins (ransomware gets them too).

steps.title: Resolution path
steps.body: Client resolver cache (and hosts file) → configured DNS server → if not authoritative: forwarders or root hints → answer cached for the record's TTL.

steps.title: Zones and records

steps.title: Aging & scavenging
steps.body: Defaults: no-refresh 7 days + refresh 7 days. Dynamic records older than both intervals can be scavenged once scavenging is enabled on the zone and a server. Static records are never scavenged.

steps.body: Pointing DCs or clients at public DNS (breaks AD); making CNAMEs at the zone apex; forgetting PTR records for services that check reverse lookups.

scenes.text: 120 laptops arrive on the 3rd floor every morning. Each needs an address, gateway and DNS without anyone typing.

steps.title: DORA
steps.body: **Discover** (client broadcast) → **Offer** (server proposes an IP) → **Request** (client asks for it) → **Acknowledge** (server confirms). Relay agents (ip helper-address on the router) forward the broadcasts across subnets to the DHCP server.

steps.title: Leases
steps.body: Windows Server's default lease is 8 days. Clients try to renew at 50% of the lease (T1) with the original server and at 87.5% (T2) with any server. Short leases (e.g. 8 hours) suit guest Wi-Fi with many transient devices.

steps.title: Scope sizing
steps.body: Range 10.30.3.100–10.30.3.250 contains 250 − 100 + 1 = 151 addresses. With 120 laptops + 18 phones + printers on reservations, it is close to full — plan exclusions and growth.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting the +1 when counting a range; overlapping scopes on two servers without failover (duplicate addresses).

steps.title: Modes

steps.title: Two gates
steps.body: Over the network, a user passes the **share** permission gate and then the **NTFS** gate. Effective access = the **more restrictive** of the two. Locally (on the server console) only NTFS applies.

steps.title: Within each layer
steps.body: Permissions from multiple groups **add up** (Read + Modify = Modify) — except an explicit **Deny** wins over Allow at the same level. Explicit permissions beat inherited ones.

steps.title: Modern practice
steps.body: Set share permissions to Authenticated Users: Full Control (or Change) and control access with NTFS groups. One place to manage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Granting users directly instead of groups; using Deny for 'Everyone' which also hits admins.

lessons.title: Lab: Root-cause analysis

scenes.text: Post-incident review for the DNS zone deletion. 'Human error' is not a root cause.
Your job now: work through it like a real engineer — gather evidence first, change one thing at a time, and write down what you did.

steps.title: 5 Whys
steps.body: Zone deleted → why? Admin ran cleanup → why? Ticket asked to remove 'old zones' → why was contoso.local in the list? Exported list included all zones, unfiltered → why no check? No peer review/change for DNS deletions → why? DNS changes considered 'routine'. **Root cause:** no change control or safeguards for destructive DNS operations.

steps.title: Actions
steps.body: Corrective (restore), preventive (change control, ProtectedFromAccidentalDeletion, least privilege), detective (alert on zone deletions). Assign owners and dates.

steps.title: How L2/L3 engineers approach it

- Define scope first: one user, one site, or everyone?
- Ask **what changed** (changes, patches, moves) — most incidents follow a change.

a.text: The draft PIR says 'Root cause: human error by admin.tom'. Accept?

choices.label: No — ask 'why' until you reach the process/control gap
Yes, and remove his admin rights
choices.feedback: Blame hides the systemic gap; it will happen again.

b.text: You find: no change required for DNS deletions, no peer review, no deletion protection, no alerting. Which actions?

choices.label: Change control for destructive DNS ops + deletion protection + alerting, each with owner/date
Send an email reminding everyone to be careful

choices.label: Add the three controls with owners

bad.text: Six months later another admin deletes a reverse zone the same way.

good.text: PIR approved: controls in place within two weeks, zone deletions now alert the AD team.
